reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with dysphagia and non-cardiac chest pain, often with a sensation of food sticking retrosternally
Defined manometrically by at least one swallow with markedly elevated contractile vigour (very high distal contractile integral), often with repetitive or vigorous multi-peaked contractions
Unlike spasm, contractions are excessively strong but retain normal or near-normal timing and propagation
Symptoms can fluctuate and may overlap with reflux and with spastic motility disorders
Outlet obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction should be excluded, as hypercontractility can be a compensatory response
Management uses smooth-muscle relaxants and neuromodulators, with peroral endoscopic myotomy considered in selected refractory cases
The finding may be an incidental manometric pattern in some patients with few symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Jackhammer oesophagus is a hypercontractile motility disorder in which the smooth-muscle segment of the oesophagus generates abnormally forceful, high-amplitude, and often repetitive contractions. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve excessive cholinergic drive and altered inhibitory neural control, sometimes as a compensatory response to distal outflow resistance at the oesophagogastric junction. The exaggerated contractile force is captured on high-resolution manometry as a very high distal contractile integral and correlates with episodes of chest pain and dysphagia.
additionalDifferentials: Achalasia with preserved or exaggerated contractility
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution oesophageal manometry to quantify contractile vigour and pattern
Upper endoscopy to exclude mucosal disease and mechanical obstruction
Timed barium oesophagram to assess emptying and morphology
Cardiac assessment to exclude ischaemic chest pain
Functional lumen imaging or reflux monitoring in selected cases
redFlags: Chest pain indistinguishable from cardiac ischaemia
Progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting obstruction or malignancy
Coexisting outflow obstruction that changes management
reference.prognosis: The natural history is variable; many patients respond to pharmacological and neuromodulatory therapy, while a subset have persistent symptoms, and a minority evolve towards a spastic achalasia phenotype.
pitfalls: Treating the manometric label rather than correlating with symptoms
Overlooking oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction driving the hypercontractility
Confusing it with distal spasm, which has abnormal contraction timing rather than excessive vigour
Attributing chest pain to the oesophagus before excluding cardiac disease
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Chicago Classification of oesophageal motility disorders
management: Smooth-muscle relaxants such as calcium-channel blockers or nitrates to reduce contractile vigour and relieve chest pain and dysphagia
Neuromodulators, including tricyclic antidepressants and other visceral analgesics, for pain modulation and oesophageal hypersensitivity
Identify and treat coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux with proton-pump inhibitors
Exclude and relieve outflow obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction, as hypercontractility may be a compensatory response
Peroral endoscopic myotomy considered in selected refractory cases
Botulinum toxin injection as an alternative endoscopic therapy in refractory disease
Reassurance with dietary and lifestyle measures, given the often benign and fluctuating course
